Ibn al-Haytham finished his Book of Optics in Cairo in the 1020s. Around 1200 it was translated into Latin under the name Alhazen: Roger Bacon used it, Witelo rewrote it at length, and John Peckham made a students' textbook out of it. Kepler's own optics of 1604 is titled as a set of additions to Witelo, and corrects Ibn al-Haytham on how the eye forms an image while working entirely inside the tradition his book began.

The numerals reached the Arabic speaking world from India, and split into two families of shapes. The western set, called ghubar or dust figures after the boards they were written on, is the one Europe learned: Gerbert of Aurillac met them in Catalonia in the tenth century, and Fibonacci learned them properly in Bugia.

In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, crossed the Sahara for the hajj with a very large caravan. On the way home he recruited scholars and an architect from Granada, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who worked at Timbuktu and Gao; the Djinguereber mosque at Timbuktu dates from that return. European mapmakers, hearing the reports, began drawing a king with a gold nugget in the middle of Africa.

How a hadith was checked. Every report carries a chain of who heard it from whom, back to the Prophet صلى الله عليه وسلم, and the chain was examined name by name: did this person exist, did they overlap in time with the one they quote, were they held to be reliable. What came out was graded sound, good or weak, and the weak ones were named as weak rather than quietly dropped.

Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara in 810 and died in 870. He travelled through Khurasan, Iraq, the Hijaz, Syria and Egypt collecting reports of what the Prophet ﷺ said and did, and interrogating the people who transmitted them: where they lived, whether they had actually met their teacher, whether anyone doubted their memory. Weighing a chain of names before weighing the text is one of the earliest systematic methods for testing testimony.

Ibn al-Nadim gives no first name, no instrument by her is known to survive, and nothing further about her life has been found. Modern accounts often call her Mariam, which is a later addition rather than anything the source says. What the single line does establish is that a woman making precision instruments in tenth century Aleppo was worth listing without comment, alongside the men. An asteroid is named al-Ijliya after her.

Indian astronomers called the half chord jya. Carried into Arabic by sound as jiba, which means nothing, it was written without vowels and read as jayb, a real word for a fold. The Latin translator rendered the meaning he found, sinus, and English shortened it to sine. The function is Indian; the name is an accident.

The Canon is five books: principles, some eight hundred simple drugs, diseases organ by organ, diseases of the whole body, and a formulary. Its success was organisation: a physician could find the passage he needed, which made it teachable. That was also the trouble with it. A book good enough to be the syllabus is a book people stop testing, and physicians from Ibn al-Nafis onward had to argue against it.

Altair and Vega are two birds on opposite banks of the Milky Way. Aldebaran follows the Pleiades. Betelgeuse is usually explained as a copyist's misreading of the Arabic for the hand of the Jawza. When the International Astronomical Union began fixing official spellings in 2016, a large share of the list was Arabic.

On 1 September 1908 the first train from Damascus reached Madinah, about 1,300 kilometres to the south, cutting a camel route of some forty days to under four. Much of the labour was done by Ottoman soldiers. It is often recounted that near Madinah the rails were laid on felt so that the noise would not disturb the Prophet's ﷺ resting place. The line ran for less than a decade before the First World War.

In 638 plague broke out at Amwas in Syria. Umar ibn al-Khattab, travelling towards Syria, halted at Sargh on the border and ordered the return. Asked whether he was fleeing the decree of Allah, he answered that he was fleeing from the decree of Allah to the decree of Allah. The rule cuts both ways, and Muslim authorities cited it again in 2020.

Ali Qushji learned his astronomy at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand, and after Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 he moved west; in the early 1470s Mehmed II brought him to Istanbul to teach. He argued that astronomy does not need Aristotle's physics underneath it and should be built on observation and geometry alone. He did not claim the earth moves. He said the case that it does not was weaker than people assumed.

Ibn al-Nafis argued that the wall between the two sides of the heart is solid and no blood seeps through it. A Venetian physician, Andrea Alpago, had spent about thirty years in Damascus and translated him into Latin, printed in Venice in the 1540s, so a channel existed. No European text of the period cites him, and independent rediscovery is entirely possible. Historians have argued both sides since an Egyptian doctor found the Arabic passage in a Berlin manuscript in 1924.
